The Rufous-breasted piculet (Picumnus rufiventris) is a small Neotropical woodpecker inhabiting lowland forests of the western Amazon basin. Field measurements from a captive rearing study indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably low mass of 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams], a value consistent with the extremely altricial state typical of piculet neonates. The incubation period, during which eggs are maintained at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], lasts 17 days [ab = 17 days], after which the helpless young require intensive brooding by both parents. This relatively brief incubation phase is characteristic of the Picumnus genus, where small clutch sizes offset the energetic demands of provisioning rapidly developing nestlings. The initial mass of the hatchling represents less than seven percent of the ultimate adult female body weight, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed during the subsequent nestling period.

Females of this species attain an ultimate adult wet weight of 21 grams [Wwi = 21 grams], placing Picumnus rufiventris among the smaller members of the Picidae family. This modest body size imposes constraints on several life-history parameters, including metabolic rate and reproductive output. Under the elevated thermal conditions typical of an actively foraging adult, which correspond to a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the species exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic demand, though modest in absolute terms, represents a relatively high mass-specific oxygen consumption compared to larger picid species, reflecting the allometric scaling of metabolism in small endotherms. The energetic cost of maintaining such a high metabolic rate likely influences both foraging behavior and the timing of critical life-history transitions.

Under the typical thermal conditions of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the developmental schedule of the nestling period is tightly constrained, with young birds achieving fledging at 23.5 days after hatching [tx = 23.5 days after hatching]. This relatively brief nestling phase is followed by a period of post-fledging dependence during which juveniles continue to receive food from their parents while refining their foraging skills. Subsequent maturation proceeds gradually, with the onset of reproductive capability occurring at 70.5 days after hatching [tp = 70.5 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This timing of sexual maturity is relatively accelerated for a picid of this size, although it reflects the general pattern observed among small-bodied woodpeckers where early reproduction is favored by high adult mortality rates and intense competition for limited nesting cavities.

Reproductive investment in Picumnus rufiventris follows a strategy typical of small altricial birds, where females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and may initiate up to 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 2.5 clutches per year] during favorable conditions. This annual reproductive output, based on comparative data from the closely related Picumnus nebulosus, yields a maximum daily reproduction rate that is modest but sustained over a lengthy breeding season. The age at first brood, representing the time elapsed since hatching at which a female produces her first successful clutch, has been recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This deferral of first reproduction until the second calendar year is a common life-history pattern among small picids, allowing females to attain full skeletal maturity and establish a breeding territory before committing to the substantial energetic costs of egg production and parental care.

Longevity records for the Rufous-breasted piculet indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] when individuals are maintained under the typical active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, unusual for such a small-bodied bird, may be linked to the species' reliance on a stable cavity-nesting strategy that reduces predation risk during the vulnerable breeding period.
